pos: n. (admission into a presence; rendering Greek prosagoge)
etymology: From Latin accedere, to approach. The Greek prosagoge is a court word — the act of being brought in and presented to a king.
biblical_def: Access is admission into a presence. Paul makes it the first fruit of justification: “being justified by faith, we have peace with God… by whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand” (Rom 5:1–2). Ephesians states it twice, once of Jew and Gentile together — “through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father” (Eph 2:18) — and once of boldness: “in whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him” (Eph 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines access as a coming to; near approach; admittance; admission; means of approach; and liberty to approach.
webster_full: ACCESS, n. A coming to; near approach; admittance; admission; as, to gain access to a prince.
2. Approach, or the way by which a thing may be approached.
3. Means of approach; liberty to approach; implying previous obstacles.
scriptures: Rom 5:2
By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
Eph 2:18
For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.
Eph 3:12
In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him.
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,
corruption_summary: Prayer is approached as though admission were still in question, and the New Testament treats access as a settled standing purchased once.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's definition contains the word the doctrine turns on: liberty to approach, implying previous obstacles. Access is only meaningful where there was a barrier, and Ephesians names the two that fell — the enmity between God and man, and the middle wall of partition between Jew and Gentile. Both were removed by one cross, which is why Paul says we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.

Hebrews 10:19-22 supplies the manner: having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus… let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith. The holiest was the room no one entered but the high priest, once a year, with blood. Ordinary believers are told to walk in, and the boldness is grounded not in their worthiness but in the blood named in the same sentence.
roots_summary: Greek prosagoge (G4318), access, introduction — a court term for being presented; parrhesia (G3954), boldness of speech.
roots_lines: Greek prosagoge (G4318) — access, introduction; Romans 5:2, Ephesians 2:18, 3:12.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom to speak; Ephesians 3:12, Hebrews 10:19.
Greek proserchomai (G4334) — to draw near; Hebrews 4:16, let us therefore come boldly.
usage: “We have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand” — the first fruit of justification.
“We both have access by one Spirit unto the Father” — two barriers, one cross.
“Boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus” — the room no one entered.

pos: n. (capacity, power to act; rendering Hebrew koach, Greek dunamis)
etymology: From Latin habilis, apt, able. Ability in Scripture is a measure God assigns and by which He apportions responsibility.
biblical_def: Ability is capacity to act. The talents are distributed “to every man according to his several ability” (Mat 25:15) — the master's apportioning removes any excuse based on comparison. The disciples in Antioch send relief “every man according to his ability” (Act 11:29). Peter says let him that ministers do it “as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified” (1Pe 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ability as physical power, whether bodily or mental; natural or acquired; force of understanding; skill in arts or science; and financial ability, the means or resources.
webster_full: ABILITY, n. Physical power, whether bodily or mental; natural or acquired; force of understanding; skill in arts or science.
2. The moral power of doing.
3. Civil or legal qualification.
4. Riches, wealth, substance, which are the means, or instruments of doing.
scriptures: And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.
Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea:

If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God; if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.
corruption_summary: Service is calibrated to what others are doing, and both the talents and the Antioch collection measure it by each man's own assigned ability.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 25:15 removes the ground of comparison before the parable begins: unto one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one; to every man according to his several ability. The distribution was neither arbitrary nor equal; it was calibrated. When the reckoning comes, the two-talent man receives word for word the same commendation as the five-talent man — well done, thou good and faithful servant — because the measure is proportion, not total.

1 Peter 4:11 closes the loop on why: if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ. Ability is supplied rather than possessed, which means both boasting and despair misread the arrangement. A servant using a supplied capacity has nothing to be proud of and no reason to be ashamed.
roots_summary: Hebrew koach (H3581), strength, ability; Greek dunamis (G1411), power; euporeo (G2141), to have means, in Acts 11:29.
roots_lines: Greek dunamis (G1411) — power, ability; Matthew 25:15, 2 Corinthians 1:8.
Greek ischus (G2479) — strength, ability; 1 Peter 4:11.
Hebrew koach (H3581) — strength, power, ability; Ezra 2:69, Leviticus 27:8.
usage: “To every man according to his several ability” — comparison removed at the start.
“Every man according to his ability” — the Antioch relief measured by each giver.
“As of the ability which God giveth” — supplied, not possessed.

pos: v. (annulled, done away; rendering Greek katargeo)
etymology: From Latin abolere, to destroy. The Greek katargeo means to render inoperative — to leave a thing in place while stripping its power.
biblical_def: To be abolished is to be annulled. Paul says Christ “hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2Ti 1:10). Ephesians says He abolished “in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” to make one new man of two (Eph 2:15). And of the fading glory on Moses' face, Paul says the children of Israel could not look to the end of “that which is abolished” (2Co 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abolish as to make void; to annul; to abrogate; and to destroy, or put an end to.
webster_full: ABOLISH, v.t. To make void; to annul; to abrogate; applied chiefly and appropriately to established laws, contracts, rites, customs and institutions.
2. To destroy, or put an end to; as to abolish idols.
scriptures: But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:
Eph 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished:
The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.
corruption_summary: Death is still described by Christians as the end, and Paul says it has been abolished — left standing as an experience while stripped of its power.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Timothy 1:10 makes a claim that sounds false to observation: Christ hath abolished death. People plainly still die. The Greek helps — katargeo is to render inoperative rather than to remove, and the second half of the verse supplies the mechanism: and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. Death remains an event and has ceased to be a destination. Paul says elsewhere that the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, so the abolition is real and its final execution is scheduled.

Ephesians 2:15 uses the same verb of the ceremonial barrier: having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace. The purpose clause matters. The abolition was not an act of dismissal toward the law but the means of forming one people out of two, which is what the whole chapter is about.
roots_summary: Greek katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, abolish; the same verb for charity never faileth and for the law's ordinances.
roots_lines: Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle, abolish; 2 Timothy 1:10, Ephesians 2:15, 2 Corinthians 3:7-14, 1 Corinthians 13:8.
Greek aphtharsia (G861) — immortality, incorruption; 2 Timothy 1:10.
Greek echthra (G2189) — enmity; Ephesians 2:15-16, abolished in his flesh.
usage: “Hath abolished death, and hath brought life… to light” — an event, no longer a destination.
“Abolished in his flesh the enmity” — the means of making one new man.
“That which is abolished” — the fading glory Moses veiled.

pos: n. (the office of an apostle; rendering Greek apostole)
etymology: From apostle, Greek apostolos, one sent with authority. Apostleship is the office rather than the man — a commission with defined limits.
biblical_def: Apostleship is the apostolic office. The eleven pray over Matthias' selection: that he “may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell” (Act 1:25). Paul says he received “grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations” (Rom 1:5), and calls the Corinthians “the seal of mine apostleship in the Lord” (1Co 9:2). Galatians notes that He who wrought effectually in Peter “to the apostleship of the circumcision” was mighty in Paul toward the Gentiles (Gal 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apostleship as the office or dignity of an apostle.
webster_full: APOSTLESHIP, n. The office or dignity of an apostle.
APOSTLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; but appropriately, a disciple of Christ commissioned to preach the gospel.
scriptures: Act 1:25
That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place.
Rom 1:5
By whom we have received grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations, for his name:
If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord.
Gal 2:8
(For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles:)
corruption_summary: The title is claimed freely today, and the New Testament attaches it to a commission with witnesses, credentials, and a stated purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 1:21-22 states the qualification for the office plainly: of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us… must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection. Eyewitness of the risen Christ, from John's baptism onward. That is a requirement no one alive can now meet, which is why the office as Luke describes it is not open.

1 Corinthians 9:2 gives Paul's own evidence, and it is not a title but a congregation: if I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord. The proof he offers is a church that exists because he preached. Romans 1:5 gives the purpose: grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations. The office was for obedience among nations, not for standing among Christians.
roots_summary: Greek apostole (G651), apostleship, a sending; apostolos (G652), one sent; sphragis (G4973), a seal — Paul's proof.
roots_lines: Greek apostole (G651) — apostleship; Acts 1:25, Romans 1:5, 1 Corinthians 9:2, Galatians 2:8.
Greek apostolos (G652) — apostle, sent one; Luke 6:13, Ephesians 4:11.
Greek sphragis (G4973) — seal, proof; 1 Corinthians 9:2, the seal of mine apostleship.
usage: “This ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell” — an office, vacated and filled.
“Grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations” — the stated purpose.
“The seal of mine apostleship are ye” — a church offered as the credential.

pos: n. (settled inclination of heart; rendering Greek phroneo and pathos)
etymology: From Latin afficere, to influence. An affection is what the heart is set upon — and Scripture commands where it is to be set.
biblical_def: Affection is settled inclination. Paul commands its direction: “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Col 3:2). He describes the redeemed as those who “have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24). Romans 1 records affections given over — “God gave them up unto vile affections” (Rom 1:26) — and Paul writes of his own toward the Thessalonians, being affectionately desirous of them (1Th 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines affection as the state of being affected; and passion, bent of mind towards a particular object, having a tendency to it; also love, kindness, good will.
webster_full: AFFECTION, n. The state of being affected.

2. Passion; but more generally, a bent of mind towards a particular object, holding a middle place between disposition, which is natural, and passion, which is excited by the presence of its exciting object.
3. In a more particular sense, a settled good will, love or zealous attachment.
scriptures: Col 3:2
Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Gal 5:24
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
Rom 1:26
For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature:
Col 3:1
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
corruption_summary: Affections are treated as involuntary weather, and Paul issues them as a command — set your affection — which assumes they can be aimed.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 3:2 is an imperative about the heart's direction: set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. That is only sensible if affections can be directed, which the whole New Testament assumes. The grounding comes first in verse 1 — if ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above — so the command is addressed to people whose position has already changed. Aiming the heart is response, not achievement.

Romans 1:26 shows the alternative and it is judicial rather than accidental: for this cause God gave them up unto vile affections. The affections were not merely disordered; they were released to their own course as a sentence. That is the most sobering thing Scripture says about desire — that being handed over to it is itself a judgment, and that it feels like freedom from the inside.
roots_summary: Greek phroneo (G5426), to set the mind on; pathos (G3806), passion; pathema (G3804), affection, in Galatians 5:24.
roots_lines: Greek phroneo (G5426) — to mind, set affection on; Colossians 3:2, Philippians 3:19, who mind earthly things.
Greek pathos (G3806) — passion, vile affection; Romans 1:26, Colossians 3:5.
Greek pathema (G3804) — affection, suffering; Galatians 5:24, Romans 7:5.
usage: “Set your affection on things above” — a command, therefore aimable.
“Have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” — executed, not managed.
“God gave them up unto vile affections” — release as sentence.

pos: n. (overbearing pride; rendering Hebrew gaon and zadon)
etymology: From Latin arrogare, to claim for oneself. Arrogancy is pride that has moved from opinion into claim.
biblical_def: Arrogancy is overbearing pride. Hannah's song forbids it: “Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed” (1Sa 2:3). Proverbs lists it among what wisdom hates: “Pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate” (Pro 8:13). Isaiah promises God will “cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease” (Isa 13:11), and Jeremiah names Moab's (Jer 48:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines arrogance or arrogancy as the act or quality of taking much upon one's self; that species of pride which consists in exorbitant claims of rank, dignity, estimation or power.
webster_full: ARROGANCE, ARROGANCY, n. The act or quality of taking much upon one's self; that species of pride which consists in exorbitant claims of rank, dignity, estimation, or power, or which exalts the worth or importance of the person to an undue degree; presumption; haughtiness.
scriptures: Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.
Pro 8:13
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible.
We have heard the pride of Moab, (he is exceeding proud) his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart.
corruption_summary: Confidence is trained as a professional asset, and Hannah's song answers arrogant speech with a fact about God rather than an argument about the speaker.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 2:3 does not tell Peninnah she is wrong about the facts; it tells her something about God: talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed. The cure for boastful speech is the existence of an accurate Judge. Where actions are weighed by One who knows, self-advertisement is not merely unattractive but pointless.

Proverbs 8:13 puts arrogancy inside a definition: the fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate. Reverence toward God is defined here by what it hates, and pride heads the list. That is why arrogance and genuine worship cannot occupy the same person for long — each is the other's solvent.
roots_summary: Hebrew gaon (H1347), exaltation, pride; zadon (H2087), presumption, arrogance; athaq (H6277), arrogant speech, in 1 Samuel 2:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew gaon (H1347) — pride, arrogancy; Proverbs 8:13, Isaiah 13:11, Jeremiah 48:29.
Hebrew athaq (H6277) — arrogant, hard speech; 1 Samuel 2:3, Psalm 31:18.
Hebrew takan (H8505) — to weigh, measure; by him actions are weighed.
usage: “Let not arrogancy come out of your mouth” — answered by a fact about God.
“By him actions are weighed” — why self-advertisement is pointless.
“Pride, and arrogancy… do I hate” — reverence defined by what it hates.

pos: n. (stunned amazement; also desolation; rendering Hebrew shammah)
etymology: From Latin attonare, to thunderstrike. To be astonished is to be struck as by thunder — the Hebrew adds the sense of a place left desolate.
biblical_def: Astonishment is stunned amazement, and in the prophets a state of desolation. Jeremiah warns that Judah shall become “an astonishment, and an hissing” among the nations (Jer 25:9). Moses lists it among covenant curses: “the LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart” (Deu 28:28). In the Gospels the crowds are astonished at Christ's doctrine, “for he taught them as one having authority” (Mat 7:28–29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines astonishment as amazement; confusion of mind from fear, surprise or admiration, at an extraordinary or unexpected event.
webster_full: ASTONISHMENT, n. Amazement; confusion of mind from fear, surprise or admiration, at an extraordinary or unexpected event.
scriptures: Mat 7:28
And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine:
Mat 7:29
For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Jer 25:9

Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the LORD, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations.
The LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart:
corruption_summary: Familiarity with Scripture is treated as maturity, and the first recorded response to Christ's preaching was that the people were astonished.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:28-29 gives the reason for the astonishment, and it is comparative: he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. The scribes taught by citation — rabbi quoting rabbi. Christ taught by assertion: but I say unto you. The crowds had heard the same texts expounded all their lives and had never heard anyone speak as though the words were his own to interpret. Astonishment was the correct response, and its absence in a congregation is worth examining.

The prophetic sense is bleaker and uses the same word for a ruined place: I will make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations. A city becomes an astonishment when passers-by stop and stare at what happened to it. Deuteronomy adds an inward version — astonishment of heart — a stunned incapacity listed among the curses, which is a different and more terrible thing than wonder.
roots_summary: Hebrew shammah (H8047), waste, astonishment; timmahon (H8541), bewilderment; Greek ekplesso (G1605), to strike out, astonish.
roots_lines: Hebrew shammah (H8047) — astonishment, desolation; Jeremiah 25:9, 11, 2 Chronicles 29:8.
Hebrew timmahon (H8541) — astonishment, bewilderment; Deuteronomy 28:28, Zechariah 12:4.
Greek ekplesso (G1605) — to be astonished, struck out; Matthew 7:28, 13:54, Mark 1:22.
usage: “The people were astonished at his doctrine” — the first response to His preaching.
“As one having authority, and not as the scribes” — the reason given.
“Astonishment of heart” — the inward version, listed as a curse.

pos: v. (to reach, arrive at; rendering Hebrew nasag, Greek katantao)
etymology: From Latin attingere, to touch upon. To attain is to reach something one was moving toward.
biblical_def: To attain is to reach. David's mighty men are ranked by it — he “attained not unto the first three” (2Sa 23:19). The psalmist says of God's knowledge, “such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it” (Psa 139:6). Paul denies having arrived: “not as though I had already attained… but I follow after” (Php 3:12), and states his aim: “if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead” (Php 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines attain as to reach; to come to or arrive at, by motion, bodily exertion, or efforts towards a place or object; and to reach or come to a place or object by progression or motion.
webster_full: ATTAIN, v.i. To reach; to come to or arrive at, by motion, bodily exertion, or efforts towards a place or object.
2. To reach; to come to or arrive at, by an effort of mind.
ATTAIN, v.t. To gain; to compass; to achieve or accomplish, that is, to reach by efforts.
scriptures: Php 3:12
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
Php 3:11
If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead.
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
Was he not most honourable of three? therefore he was their captain: howbeit he attained not unto the first three.
corruption_summary: Spiritual maturity is claimed as a plateau reached, and the most mature man in the New Testament wrote that he had not attained.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 3:12 is written by a man near the end of an extraordinary life: not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. The clause that steadies it is the last one — he pursues because he was first laid hold of. The pursuit is response to a prior apprehension, not an attempt to secure one.

Psalm 139:6 shows a different kind of unattainable: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it. Here the failure to reach is not a deficiency to be remedied but a fact to be worshipped. Some things are pursued because they can be reached; others are confessed unreachable and adored. Confusing the two categories produces either despair or presumption.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasag (H5381), to reach, overtake; Greek katantao (G2658), to arrive at; lambano (G2983), to obtain, in Philippians 3:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasag (H5381) — to reach, attain, overtake; 2 Samuel 23:19, 23, Psalm 139:6.
Greek katantao (G2658) — to attain, arrive; Philippians 3:11, Ephesians 4:13, till we all come.
Greek katalambano (G2638) — to apprehend, lay hold; Philippians 3:12-13.
usage: “Not as though I had already attained” — written near the end of that life.
“That for which also I am apprehended” — pursuit as response.
“It is high, I cannot attain unto it” — a failure to be worshipped, not remedied.

pos: n. (originator, first cause; rendering Greek archegos and aitios)
etymology: From Latin auctor, one who causes to grow. An author in Scripture is an originator — the one from whom a thing proceeds.
biblical_def: An author is an originator. Hebrews calls Christ “the author and finisher of our faith” (Heb 12:2) and “the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him” (Heb 5:9). Paul settles a disordered assembly by an argument from God's character: “God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1Co 14:33). Acts calls Christ the Prince of life, using the same Greek word (Act 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines author as one who produces, creates, or brings into being; the beginner, former, or first mover of any thing; hence, the efficient cause of a thing; and the writer of a book or treatise.
webster_full: AUTHOR, n. One who produces, creates, or brings into being; as, God is the author of the Universe.
2. The beginner, former, or first mover of any thing; hence, the efficient cause of a thing.
3. The writer of a book or treatise.
scriptures: Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Heb 5:9
And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him;
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Act 3:15
And killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses.
corruption_summary: Faith is spoken of as something a person generates and must sustain, and Hebrews names Christ as both its author and its finisher.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:2 brackets the whole Christian life: looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. He began it and He will complete it, which leaves the believer's part as looking. The verse comes at the end of the great chapter of examples, and after listing dozens of faithful men and women the writer turns the eyes off them and onto the One who authored what they had.

1 Corinthians 14:33 settles a practical dispute by an argument from character: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace. Paul is regulating a chaotic worship service, and rather than issuing preferences he reasons from what God is like. Any practice that reliably produces confusion in an assembly has an authorship problem, whatever spiritual claims are made for it.
roots_summary: Greek archegos (G747), originator, prince, captain; aitios (G159), cause, author — Hebrews 5:9; akatastasia (G181), confusion.
roots_lines: Greek archegos (G747) — author, prince, captain; Hebrews 12:2, 2:10, Acts 3:15, 5:31.
Greek aitios (G159) — cause, author; only Hebrews 5:9.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — confusion, tumult; 1 Corinthians 14:33, James 3:16.
usage: “The author and finisher of our faith” — both ends held by Him.
“The author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him” — origin and condition together.
“God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” — a practice judged by its fruit.

pos: n. (one who exacts blood-justice; rendering Hebrew goel haddam)
etymology: From avenge, Latin vindicare. The Hebrew is the redeemer of blood — the same word as kinsman-redeemer, in its judicial function.
biblical_def: An avenger exacts justice for blood. The law appoints cities of refuge so that a manslayer “may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares… that he die not by the hand of the avenger of blood” (Num 35:11–12). The psalmist says God ordains strength “that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger” (Psa 8:2). Paul says the magistrate “is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4), and forbids private vengeance: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines avenger as one who avenges or vindicates; a vindicator; a revenger.
webster_full: AVENGER, n. One who avenges or vindicates; a vindicator; a revenger.
AVENGE, v.t. To take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or evil on the wrongdoer.
scriptures: And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Psa 8:2
Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger.
corruption_summary: Private grievance seeks its own satisfaction, and Scripture routes vengeance through cities of refuge, appointed magistrates, and finally God Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The cities of refuge are one of the law's most humane provisions, and their necessity assumes the avenger's existence. A man who killed at unawares could run to a city and stand trial rather than be cut down by a grieving relative on the road. The system did not abolish the avenger; it interposed a court between grief and execution, and it required the manslayer to remain there until the death of the high priest.

Romans 12 and 13 are one argument and are usually separated. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves… for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay — and then, of the magistrate, he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath. Private vengeance is forbidden precisely because God has appointed a public instrument for it. The prohibition is not a denial that wrongs should be answered.
roots_summary: Hebrew goel haddam (H1350/H1818), the redeemer of blood; naqam (H5358), to avenge; Greek ekdikos (G1558), an avenger.
roots_lines: Hebrew goel haddam — avenger of blood; Numbers 35:12, 19, Deuteronomy 19:6, Joshua 20:3.
Greek ekdikos (G1558) — avenger, revenger; Romans 13:4, 1 Thessalonians 4:6.
Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — vengeance; Romans 12:19, Hebrews 10:30.
usage: “That he die not by the hand of the avenger of blood” — a court interposed between grief and execution.
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay” — the prohibition on private revenge.
“A revenger to execute wrath” — the public instrument appointed.

pos: n. pl. (infants; also the spiritually immature; rendering Greek nepios)
etymology: Middle English babe. The Greek nepios means literally not-speaking — one who cannot yet articulate, used both tenderly and as a rebuke.
biblical_def: Babes are infants, and by extension the immature. Christ thanks the Father for hiding things from the wise and prudent and revealing them “unto babes” (Mat 11:25). Paul rebukes the Corinthians: “I could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ. I have fed you with milk, and not with meat” (1Co 3:1–2). Peter commands, “as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines babe as an infant; a young child of either sex.
webster_full: BABE, n. An infant; a young child of either sex.
BABISH, a. Like a babe; childish.
scriptures: At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
corruption_summary: Being a babe is either romanticized as childlike faith or used to excuse permanent immaturity, and Scripture uses the word both approvingly and as a rebuke.
corruption_paragraphs: The two uses have to be held together or one will cancel the other. Matthew 11:25 is approving: thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes. The reception of revelation does not require sophistication, and God has arranged it so that it cannot be secured by sophistication. That is grace to the ordinary reader.

1 Corinthians 3:1-2 is a rebuke, and the tell is time: I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able. Milk is right for a new believer and wrong for one who should have moved on. Ephesians 4:14 names the danger of staying: that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine. Permanent infancy is not humility; it is vulnerability.
roots_summary: Greek nepios (G3516), an infant, one not speaking; brephos (G1025), a newborn; artigennetos (G738), newborn, in 1 Peter 2:2.
roots_lines: Greek nepios (G3516) — babe, infant, immature; Matthew 11:25, 1 Corinthians 3:1, Ephesians 4:14, Hebrews 5:13.
Greek artigennetos (G738) — newborn; only 1 Peter 2:2.
Greek logikos (G3050) — of the word, reasonable; the sincere milk of the word.
usage: “Hast revealed them unto babes” — revelation not secured by sophistication.
“I have fed you with milk, and not with meat” — right food, wrong stage.
“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word” — appetite as the sign of life.

pos: n. (enforced exile; rendering Aramaic sheroshu, Hebrew madduach)
etymology: From Old French banir, to proclaim as an outlaw. Banishment is exile imposed by authority — and Scripture records it as a penalty and as a false prophecy.
biblical_def: Banishment is enforced exile. Artaxerxes authorizes Ezra to impose it among other penalties: “whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment” (Ezr 7:26). Lamentations charges the false prophets with having seen for Judah “false burdens and causes of banishment” (Lam 2:14). David's estrangement from Absalom uses the related idea: “that his banished be not expelled from him” (2Sa 14:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines banishment as the act of a prince or magistrate compelling a citizen to leave his own country; and the state of being banished, exile.
webster_full: BANISHMENT, n. The act of a prince or competent authority, compelling a citizen to leave his own country, or to reside in a particular place, in the same country.
2. The state of being banished; exile.
3. The act of driving away or dispelling.
scriptures: Ezr 7:26

And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment. to banishment: Chaldee, to rooting out
Lam 2:14
Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment.

For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him.
Lam 2:9
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD.
corruption_summary: Comfortable preaching is judged by whether people liked it, and Lamentations judges it by what it failed to prevent — banishment.
corruption_paragraphs: Lamentations 2:14 is the harshest thing Scripture says about pleasant preaching: thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment. The charge is not that they lied about the future but that they failed to expose present sin, and the omission is named as a cause of exile. Preaching that never discovers iniquity is not neutral; it is implicated in what follows.

2 Samuel 14:14 contains one of the most surprising theological sentences in the historical books, spoken by a woman of Tekoa to David: for we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him. God is described as contriving ways to bring back the exiled — a sentence that reaches far past Absalom.
roots_summary: Aramaic sheroshi (H8332), banishment, rooting out; Hebrew madduach (H4065), a cause of banishment; nadach (H5080), to drive away.
roots_lines: Aramaic sheroshu (H8332) — banishment, uprooting; only Ezra 7:26.
Hebrew madduach (H4065) — cause of banishment; only Lamentations 2:14.
Hebrew nadach (H5080) — to drive out, banish; 2 Samuel 14:13-14, his banished.
usage: “Whether it be unto death, or to banishment” — a Persian king's grant of penalties.
“False burdens and causes of banishment” — comfortable preaching implicated in exile.
“He devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him” — God contriving return.

pos: n. (benefit, superiority; rendering Greek perissos and opheleo)
etymology: From Old French avantage, from avant, before. An advantage is a position ahead of another — and Paul asks whether being a Jew confers one.
biblical_def: Advantage is benefit. Paul raises the question directly: “What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:1–2). Christ asks, “what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself?” (Luk 9:25). Paul warns against Satan getting an advantage over the church through unforgiveness (2Co 2:11), and Jude says some have men's persons in admiration “because of advantage” (Jud 16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines advantage as any state, condition, or circumstance, favorable to success, prosperity, interest, or reputation; benefit; gain; profit.
webster_full: ADVANTAGE, n. Any state, condition, or circumstance, favorable to success, prosperity, interest, or reputation.
2. Benefit; gain; profit.
3. Means to an end; opportunity; convenience for obtaining benefit.
scriptures: Rom 3:1
What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision?
Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
Luk 9:25
For what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away?
Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices.
corruption_summary: Privilege is either denied or treated as merit, and Paul says the Jew's advantage was real, was enormous, and consisted in being trusted with something.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 3:1-2 handles privilege with unusual care. Paul has just dismantled every ground of Jewish confidence, and then asks the obvious question: what advantage then hath the Jew? His answer is not none — it is much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. The advantage was real and it was a trust rather than a status. Being given something to keep is a privilege that increases accountability rather than standing.

2 Corinthians 2:11 names an advantage of a different kind: lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices. The context is restoring a disciplined member who had repented. Paul's concern is that a church which refuses to forgive hands the adversary a position, and he treats prolonged unforgiveness in a congregation as a tactical loss rather than merely a personal failing.
roots_summary: Greek perissos (G4053), superiority, advantage; opheleo (G5623), to profit; pleonekteo (G4122), to get an advantage over.
roots_lines: Greek perissos (G4053) — advantage, abundance; Romans 3:1.
Greek pleonekteo (G4122) — to get an advantage, overreach; 2 Corinthians 2:11, 7:2, 12:17-18.
Greek opheleia (G5622) — profit, advantage; Jude 16, Romans 3:1.
usage: “Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God” — privilege as trust.
“What is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world?” — the accounting question.
“Lest Satan should get an advantage of us” — unforgiveness as a tactical loss.

pos: adj. (plentiful, overflowing; rendering Greek perisseuo)
etymology: From Latin abundare, to overflow — literally to rise in waves. Abundance in Scripture is overflow rather than sufficiency.
biblical_def: Abundant means overflowing. God proclaims Himself to Moses as “abundant in goodness and truth” (Exo 34:6). Peter blesses God who “according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1Pe 1:3). Paul says grace “was exceeding abundant with faith and love” toward him, the chief of sinners (1Ti 1:14), and Christ came that they might have life “more abundantly” (Joh 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abundant as plentiful; in great quantity; fully sufficient; and abounding, having in great quantity.
webster_full: ABUNDANT, a. Plentiful; in great quantity; fully sufficient; as an abundant supply.
2. Abounding; having in great quantity; fully stored.
ABUNDANCE, n. Great plenty; an overflowing quantity; ample sufficiency.
scriptures: Exo 34:6
And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
corruption_summary: Abundant life is quoted as a promise of circumstances, and Christ says it in a chapter about a shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
corruption_paragraphs: John 10:10 is one of the most misquoted verses in Scripture. I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly — and the very next sentence is I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. The abundance is defined by what follows, not by what a reader hopes. The chapter's contrast is with a thief who comes to steal, kill, and destroy, and with a hireling who runs. Abundant life means life under a Shepherd who stays and dies.

Exodus 34:6 is God's own self-description and the abundance named is moral: merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth. This is the verse quoted back to God more often than any other in the Old Testament — by Moses, David, Jonah, Joel, Nehemiah — because it is what He said about Himself when asked to show His glory.
roots_summary: Greek perisseuo (G4052), to overflow, abound; polus (G4183), much; Hebrew rab (H7227), abundant, great.
roots_lines: Hebrew rab (H7227) — abundant, great; Exodus 34:6, abundant in goodness and truth.
Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, overflow; John 10:10, 2 Corinthians 9:8.
Greek huperpleonazo (G5250) — to superabound; 1 Timothy 1:14, exceeding abundant.
usage: “Abundant in goodness and truth” — God's own self-description.
“According to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again” — the new birth's measure.
“That they might have it more abundantly” — defined by the Shepherd who dies.

pos: v. (decorated, made fitting; rendering Greek kosmeo)
etymology: From Latin adornare, to fit out. The Greek kosmeo gives us cosmetic and cosmos — to adorn is to bring into order, not merely to decorate.
biblical_def: To be adorned is to be fittingly ordered. Paul tells servants to be faithful “that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things” (Tit 2:10) — ordinary honesty making a teaching attractive. Peter directs adorning inward: “whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning… but let it be the hidden man of the heart… even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:3–4). John sees the holy city “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines adorn as to deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress; to deck with external ornaments; and to display the beauty or excellence of.
webster_full: ADORN, v.t. To deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress; to deck with external ornaments.
2. To set off to advantage; to add ornaments to; to embellish by any thing external or adventitious.
3. To display the beauty or excellence of.
scriptures: Tit 2:10
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Rev 21:2
And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
corruption_summary: Doctrine is defended by argument alone, and Paul assigns its adorning to household servants doing their work honestly.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 2:10 gives an unexpected assignment. Paul is addressing bondservants — the least powerful people in the congregation — and tells them not to purloin, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things. The doctrine is adorned not by scholars but by servants who do not steal. A teaching is made attractive by lives that fit it, and the lowest-status members of a church have the most direct access to that work.

1 Peter 3:4 supplies the valuation that makes inward adorning worth the trouble: the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. Peter does not say outward adorning is worthless; he says the priority is inverted. And he settles the question of value by naming whose appraisal counts — in the sight of God.
roots_summary: Greek kosmeo (G2885), to arrange, adorn — from kosmos, order; kosmos (G2889), adornment or world; polutelēs (G4185), of great price.
roots_lines: Greek kosmeo (G2885) — to adorn, set in order; Titus 2:10, 1 Peter 3:5, Revelation 21:2, Matthew 25:7.
Greek kosmos (G2889) — adorning, order, world; 1 Peter 3:3.
Greek polutelēs (G4185) — very costly; 1 Peter 3:4, of great price.
usage: “That they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour” — assigned to servants.
“The hidden man of the heart… of great price” — the appraisal that counts.
“As a bride adorned for her husband” — the city made ready.

pos: v. (to correct, make better; rendering Hebrew yatab, Greek echo kompsoteron)
etymology: From Latin emendare, to free from fault. To amend is to correct what is wrong rather than to add what is missing.
biblical_def: To amend is to correct. Jeremiah's temple sermon states the condition: “Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place” (Jer 7:3), and again, “if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour” (Jer 7:5). The nobleman's servants report that his son “began to amend” at the seventh hour (Joh 4:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amend as to correct; to rectify by expunging a mistake; to reform, by quitting bad habits; to make better in a moral sense; and to grow better by reformation.
webster_full: AMEND, v.t. To correct; to rectify by expunging a mistake; as, to amend a law.
2. To reform, by quitting bad habits; to make better in a moral sense.
3. To correct; to supply a defect; to improve or make better.
AMEND, v.i. To grow better by reformation, or rectifying something wrong in manners or morals.
scriptures: Jer 7:3
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place.
Jer 7:5
For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour;
Joh 4:52
Then enquired he of them the hour when he began to amend. And they said unto him, Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.
Jer 7:4
Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these.
corruption_summary: Attendance at the right building is treated as covering the life lived outside it, and Jeremiah 7 was preached in the temple gate to people on their way in.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 7:4 is the verse the sermon turns on: trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these. The triple repetition mimics a chant. People were treating the building's presence as a guarantee, and the prophet stood in its gate to say the guarantee did not exist. What he asked for instead was specific and unspiritual-sounding: execute judgment, oppress not the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.

The word amend rather than repent is worth noticing here. Jeremiah asks for correction of ways and doings — the ordinary conduct of ordinary life. Amendment is what repentance looks like when it reaches the hands, and the promise attached is concrete: then will I cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers.
roots_summary: Hebrew yatab (H3190), to make good, do well — the verb behind amend your ways; Greek kompsoteron echo, to have it better, in John 4:52.
roots_lines: Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to make good, amend; Jeremiah 7:3, 5, 26:13, 35:15.
Hebrew derek (H1870) and maalal (H4611) — ways and doings; the pair Jeremiah asks amended.
Greek kompsoteron (G2866) — better; only John 4:52.
usage: “Amend your ways and your doings” — correction reaching the hands.
“The temple of the LORD… are these” — a chant treated as a guarantee.
“Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him” — the hour the child began to amend.

pos: v. (estranged, made a stranger; rendering Greek apallotrioo)
etymology: From Latin alienus, belonging to another. To be alienated is to have been made foreign to something one once belonged to.
biblical_def: To be alienated is to be estranged. Paul describes the Gentile condition before Christ: “at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world” (Eph 2:12), and says they were “alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart” (Eph 4:18). Colossians says believers “were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled” (Col 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alienate as to transfer title, property or right to another; to estrange; to withdraw, as the affections; and to make indifferent or averse, where love or friendship before subsisted.
webster_full: ALIENATE, v.t. To transfer title, property or right to another.
2. To estrange; to withdraw, as the affections; to make indifferent or averse, where love or friendship before subsisted.
ALIENATED, pp. Estranged; withdrawn from; transferred to another.
scriptures: Eph 2:12
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
Eph 4:18
Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:
Col 1:21
And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled
Eph 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
corruption_summary: Estrangement from God is described as distance to be closed by effort, and Paul describes it as a settled legal and moral condition ended by a Person.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 2:12 stacks five deprivations without softening any: without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. That is the fullest description of the unconverted state in the New Testament, and it is addressed to believers about their own past. The next verse turns entirely on two words: but now — but now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.

Colossians 1:21 locates the alienation in the mind and the works: enemies in your mind by wicked works. It was not a misunderstanding awaiting explanation, nor a distance awaiting travel. It was hostility with a track record, and the remedy named is reconciliation accomplished in the body of his flesh through death — a past event, not a process the alienated party undertakes.
roots_summary: Greek apallotrioo (G526), to alienate, estrange; xenos (G3581), a stranger; katallasso (G2644), to reconcile — the reversal.
roots_lines: Greek apallotrioo (G526) — to alienate; Ephesians 2:12, 4:18, Colossians 1:21.
Greek xenos (G3581) — stranger, foreigner; Ephesians 2:12, 19, now therefore ye are no more strangers.
Greek katallasso (G2644) — to reconcile; Colossians 1:21, yet now hath he reconciled.
usage: “Aliens from the commonwealth… strangers from the covenants” — five deprivations, unsoftened.
“But now in Christ Jesus… made nigh” — the hinge of the paragraph.
“Enemies in your mind by wicked works” — hostility with a track record.

pos: v., n. (to misuse; rendering Greek katachraomai)
etymology: From Latin abuti, to use up or misuse. Abuse in the KJV is chiefly misuse — using a lawful thing wrongly.
biblical_def: To abuse is to misuse. Paul's counsel about the world uses the word precisely: “they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away” (1Co 7:31). He refuses payment so as not to “abuse my power in the gospel” (1Co 9:18). Saul, mortally wounded, fears the Philistines will “abuse” him (1Sa 31:4), and the men of Gibeah abused the Levite's concubine all night (Jdg 19:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abuse as to use ill; to maltreat; to misuse; to use with bad motives or to wrong purposes; to violate; to defile; and to deceive, to impose on.
webster_full: ABUSE, v.t. To use ill; to maltreat; to misuse; to use with bad motives or to wrong purposes.
2. To violate; to defile by improper sexual intercourse.
3. To deceive; to impose on.
4. To treat rudely, or with reproachful language; to revile.
scriptures: And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
What is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel.

Then said Saul unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it.

But the men would not hearken to him: so the man took his concubine, and brought her forth unto them; and they knew her, and abused her all the night until the morning: and when the day began to spring, they let her go.
corruption_summary: Lawful things are assumed safe because they are lawful, and Paul's warning is about abusing what may rightly be used.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 7:31 draws a fine line: they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away. The world is to be used — Paul is not prescribing withdrawal — but held loosely, because its arrangement is temporary. Abuse here is not vice but over-investment: treating a passing thing as though it would last. The whole passage is about doing ordinary business, marrying, buying, weeping and rejoicing, with a light grip.

1 Corinthians 9:18 shows Paul applying it to a right he actually possessed. He had argued at length that ministers may live of the gospel, and then declined the payment so that he might not abuse his power in the gospel. Having established the right, he surrendered its use. That combination — defend the principle, decline the benefit — is rare and worth imitating.
roots_summary: Greek katachraomai (G2710), to use fully, to misuse; alal (H5953) in Hebrew, to deal severely with, in Judges 19:25.
roots_lines: Greek katachraomai (G2710) — to use up, abuse; 1 Corinthians 7:31, 9:18.
Hebrew alal (H5953) — to abuse, deal wantonly; Judges 19:25, 1 Samuel 31:4.
Greek schema (G4976) — fashion, outward form; 1 Corinthians 7:31, the fashion of this world passeth away.
usage: “They that use this world, as not abusing it” — a light grip on a passing arrangement.
“That I abuse not my power in the gospel” — a right defended and declined.
“The fashion of this world passeth away” — the reason given.

pos: v. (to complete, fulfil; rendering Hebrew kalah, Greek teleo)
etymology: From Latin ad and complere, to fill up. To accomplish is to fill out what was begun until nothing remains outstanding.
biblical_def: To accomplish is to complete. God says of His word, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” (Isa 55:11). Daniel understands by books “the number of the years… that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem” (Dan 9:2). Luke says Moses and Elijah on the mount spoke of Christ's decease “which he should accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luk 9:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines accomplish as to complete; to finish entirely; to execute; to fulfill; to carry into effect; and to gain, to obtain or effect by successful exertions.
webster_full: ACCOMPLISH, v.t. To complete; to finish entirely.
2. To execute; as to accomplish a vow, wrath or fury.
3. To gain; to obtain or effect by successful exertions.
4. To fulfill or bring to pass; as, to accomplish a prophecy.
5. To furnish with qualities which serve to render the mind or body complete.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Dan 9:2

In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem.
Luk 9:31
Who appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.

For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:
corruption_summary: Preaching is judged by visible response, and Isaiah attaches the guarantee to the word itself rather than to the audience.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 55:11 is the preacher's warrant and it contains no clause about reception: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it. The word accomplishes what God pleases, which is not always what the speaker hoped. Isaiah himself was told to preach to people who would not hear, and the promise held for him too.

Luke 9:31 uses the word of the crucifixion, and the choice is striking: they spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem. Not suffer, not undergo — accomplish. Moses and Elijah discussed the cross with Him as a work to be completed. That single verb rules out any reading of Calvary as a tragedy that overtook Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalah (H3615), to complete, finish; tsalach (H6743), to prosper; Greek teleo (G5055), to finish; pleroo (G4137), to fulfil.
roots_lines: Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to accomplish, complete; Daniel 9:2, 2 Chronicles 36:21.
Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, accomplish; Isaiah 55:11, it shall accomplish that which I please.
Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fulfil, accomplish; Luke 9:31, Acts 13:33.
usage: “It shall accomplish that which I please” — no clause about reception.
“His decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem” — a work completed, not a fate suffered.
“He would accomplish seventy years” — Daniel reading a deadline in a book.

pos: v. (to distress, humble; rendering Hebrew anah)
etymology: From Latin affligere, to strike down. The Hebrew anah covers both being afflicted by others and afflicting one's own soul in fasting.
biblical_def: To afflict is to distress or humble. The law commands self-affliction on the day of atonement: “ye shall afflict your souls… for on that day shall the priest make an atonement for you” (Lev 16:29–30). God warns concerning the widow and fatherless, “If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry” (Exo 22:23). The psalmist testifies, “It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes” (Psa 119:71).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines afflict as to give to the body or mind pain which is continued or of some permanence; to grieve, or distress; and to trouble, to harass.
webster_full: AFFLICT, v.t. To give to the body or mind pain which is continued or of some permanence; to grieve, or distress.
2. To trouble; to harass; to distress.
scriptures: And this shall be a statute for ever unto you: that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, ye shall afflict your souls, and do no work at all, whether it be one of your own country, or a stranger that sojourneth among you:
If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry;
It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes.
Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word.
corruption_summary: Affliction is asked to be explained before it can be accepted, and the psalmist evaluates his in retrospect as good without ever receiving a reason.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 119:67 and 71 give a before and after: before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word… It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes. The psalmist does not say the affliction was pleasant or that he understood it at the time. He offers a retrospective verdict based on what it produced, and what it produced was attention to God's word that comfort had not produced.

Exodus 22:23 is one of the most alarming promises in the law, addressed to anyone tempted to exploit the powerless: if thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry. The Hebrew doubles the verbs for emphasis — if afflicting thou afflict, if crying they cry, hearing I will hear. God undertakes to be the widow's advocate personally, and the sentence that follows is severe.
roots_summary: Hebrew anah (H6031), to afflict, humble, be bowed down — the same verb for fasting and for oppression; Greek thlibo (G2346), to press.
roots_lines: Hebrew anah (H6031) — to afflict, humble; Leviticus 16:29, Exodus 22:22-23, Psalm 119:71.
Hebrew oni (H6040) — affliction; Genesis 41:52, Exodus 3:7, I have seen the affliction of my people.
Greek thlipsis (G2347) — tribulation, affliction; 2 Corinthians 4:17, our light affliction.
usage: “Ye shall afflict your souls” — the day of atonement's required humbling.
“I will surely hear their cry” — God as the widow's personal advocate.
“It is good for me that I have been afflicted” — a retrospective verdict.

pos: v. (to test and accept; rendering Greek dokimazo)
etymology: From Latin approbare, to assent to as good. The Greek dokimazo means to test metal — approval follows assay rather than preceding it.
biblical_def: To approve is to test and accept. Paul commands, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). He says of ministry, “we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts” (1Th 2:4). And the audience that matters is named plainly: “not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth” (2Co 10:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines approve as to like; to be pleased with; to admit the propriety of; to prove or show to be worthy of approbation; and to like and sustain as right.
webster_full: APPROVE, v.t. To like; to be pleased with; to admit the propriety of; as, we approve the measures of administration.
2. To prove; to show to be true; to justify.
3. To experience; to prove by trial.
4. To make or show to be worthy of approbation; to commend.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
But as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts.
For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.
For he that in these things serveth Christ is acceptable to God, and approved of men.
corruption_summary: Ministry is calibrated to audience response, and Paul's stated aim was approval by the One who tries hearts rather than by the people in front of him.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Thessalonians 2:4 states the choice starkly: not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts. Paul is not indifferent to his hearers — the same chapter compares him to a nursing mother and a father exhorting his children — but the approval he works for comes from a different quarter. Where those two audiences diverge, he had settled in advance which one he would lose.

2 Corinthians 10:18 removes self-assessment from the equation: for not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth. That cuts against both boasting and its inverse, since a man's harsh verdict on himself is no more authoritative than a flattering one. The assay is conducted elsewhere, and 2 Timothy 2:15 names the workman's part: study, and rightly divide.
roots_summary: Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test, approve after trial; dokimos (G1384), approved; sunistemi (G4921), to commend.
roots_lines: Greek dokimos (G1384) — approved, tested; 2 Timothy 2:15, Romans 14:18, 16:10.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, test; 1 Thessalonians 2:4, Romans 12:2, 1 Corinthians 11:28.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, rightly divide; only 2 Timothy 2:15.
usage: “Shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” — the aim and the means.
“Not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts” — the audience settled in advance.
“Whom the Lord commendeth” — self-assessment removed in both directions.
